notes: KDP kept in slot 5 to follow MD's KSDP placement (same organization, renamed 1981). Revolutionary Party for Reunification placed in 18, DFRF in 19 per MD. Southern refugee institutions (Committee for the Five Northern Provinces, Yongnak Church, Korea Muslim Federation) fill the Western and Islamic slots. Shia and caliphate slots use small foreign-student circles in Pyongyang.

0.name: Ibuk Odo Wiwŏnhoe
0.english: Committee for the Five Northern Korean Provinces
0.text:
The Committee for the Five Northern Korean Provinces is the shadow administration the Republic of Korea maintains in Seoul for the provinces it claims north of the 38th parallel. Created in 1949 under the Ministry of Home Affairs, it appoints titular governors for Hwanghae, Pyongan, Hamgyong and the other northern provinces and keeps registers of refugee families who fled south.

Its outlook is that of Park Chung-hee's state: unification on Seoul's terms, total hostility to the Workers' Party and close alignment with Washington. Its leverage lies with the millions of northern refugees and their associations, which supply the South's most uncompromising anti-communists and would furnish the cadres of any southern-led administration in the North.

1.name: Yŏngnak Kyohoe
1.text:
Yongnak Presbyterian Church in Seoul was founded in 1945 by Christians who fled Pyongyang and the northern provinces, once the heartland of Korean Protestantism. Under its pastor Han Kyung-chik it has grown into one of the largest congregations in Asia and the spiritual home of the northern refugee community.

The church preaches a conservative, evangelical faith fused with fierce anti-communism and the memory of churches closed and pastors arrested in the North. It looks to the United States and its missions as protectors, demands religious freedom above the 38th parallel and draws on a dense network of refugee families, schools and charities that dream of returning to rebuild the northern churches.

2.name: Yŏnan-p'a
2.text:
The Yan'an Faction is the remnant of the communists who fought alongside Mao's armies in China before returning to Korea in 1945. After the August Faction Incident of 1956, when they challenged Kim Il-sung's personality cult, most were purged; Yun Kong-hum and So Hwi escaped to China, while those who stayed behind were imprisoned or silenced.

Their programme, now kept alive only in exile and in quiet memory, calls for collective leadership, an end to the cult of the Leader, more consumer goods and a less punishing pace of heavy industry. They have no organization inside the country, but their critique resurfaces whenever cadres tire of mobilization campaigns and purges.

3.name: Chosŏn Chigŏp Ch'ongdongmaeng
3.english: General Federation of Trade Unions of Korea
3.text:
The General Federation of Trade Unions of Korea was founded in November 1945 and organizes every factory, mine and office worker in the DPRK. Like all mass organizations it operates under the direction of the Workers' Party, transmitting production targets and political study to the shop floor.

Within those limits the federation speaks for the industrial working class: wages, rations, housing and safety in the plants built during the Chollima years. It maintains ties with the World Federation of Trade Unions and fraternal unions in both Moscow and Beijing, and its leverage lies in the sheer size of the urban workforce on which the Seven-Year Plan depends.
3.wiki: General Federation of Trade Unions of Korea

4.name: Chosŏn Rodongdang
4.text:
The Workers' Party of Korea has ruled the North since its founding and is led by its General Secretary Kim Il-sung. The purges of 1967 removed the Kapsan group, and in early 1969 senior generals were dismissed after the failed raid on the Blue House, leaving the Manchurian partisan veterans around Kim in unchallenged control.

The party proclaims Juche, the doctrine of self-reliance, and the parallel build-up of the economy and national defence. It balances between Moscow and Beijing while denouncing both revisionism and dogmatism, prepares for its Fifth Congress, and commands every institution of state, army and society through its cells and the growing cult of the Leader.

5.name: Chosŏn Minjudang
5.text:
The Korean Democratic Party was founded in Pyongyang in November 1945 by the Christian nationalist Cho Man-sik as the voice of the northern middle classes and merchants. After Cho's arrest in 1946 the party was taken over by figures loyal to the communists and now exists as a junior member of the Democratic Front for the Reunification of the Fatherland.

Officially it represents small traders, intellectuals and former property owners who accept socialist construction. It holds seats in the Supreme People's Assembly and serves the regime as a showcase of multi-party unity, especially toward the South, yet its old social base remembers a time when it was the largest party in the North.

6.name: Ppalch'isan-p'a
6.text:
The Partisan Faction is the inner core of veterans who fought with Kim Il-sung in the anti-Japanese guerrilla units of Manchuria in the 1930s. Having outlasted the Soviet-Korean, Yan'an and Kapsan groups, men such as Minister of People's Armed Forces Choe Hyon and O Jin-u now dominate the army and the party's upper ranks.

They are the guardians of the guerrilla tradition: militarized society, permanent vigilance against the United States and the South, and rejection of any relaxation in the Soviet or Chinese manner. Their power rests on personal loyalty to Kim and on control of the armed forces, and they distrust technocrats who place output figures above revolutionary spirit.

7.name: Ch'ŏndogyo Ch'ŏngudang
7.text:
The Chondoist Chongu Party was founded in 1946 as the political arm of Chondoism, the indigenous Korean religion descended from the Donghak peasant movement of 1894. Once a mass party among northern farmers, it has been subordinated to the Workers' Party and sits in the Democratic Front for the Reunification of the Fatherland.

It preaches the Chondoist ideal that man is heaven, joined to anti-imperialist nationalism and loyalty to the state. Pyongyang uses it to address believers and to reach Chondoists in the South, where the faith remains organized. Its leverage is modest but symbolic, linking the regime to the native revolutionary tradition of the Donghak uprising.

8.name: Halqat al-Talaba al-'Iraqiyyin
8.text:
The Iraqi Students' Circle is a small group of Shia students from Baghdad, Najaf and Basra sent to Pyongyang after Iraq and the DPRK established diplomatic relations in 1968. Living in dormitories at Kim Il-sung University and the technical institutes, they keep their prayers and Muharram observances in private rooms.

Raised among the reformist ideas spreading from the seminaries of Najaf, they favour an Islam engaged with social justice, education and anti-colonial politics. They have no standing in Korean society, but they act as informal intermediaries for Iraqi delegations and Shia visitors, and their reports home shape how religious Iraqis perceive the Juche state.

9.name: Majlis al-Husayni
9.text:
The Husayni Gathering is the stricter core of Shia believers among the Arab students and embassy staff in Pyongyang, who meet during Ashura to mourn the martyrdom of Imam Husayn. Its members follow the senior clergy of Najaf and regard the Ba'athist government in Baghdad with growing suspicion.

They hold that religious scholars, not secular parties, must guide Muslim society, and they treat both the American and Soviet camps as godless. Their circle is tiny and closely watched by Korean security, yet it carries the uncompromising clerical politics of Najaf into the most closed state in Asia and keeps alive a network of loyalty to the marja'.

10.name: Han'guk Isŭllamgyo Chungang Yŏnhap-hoe
10.text:
The Korea Muslim Federation, organized in Seoul in 1967 from the Korea Islamic Society of 1955, represents the small Korean Muslim community that grew out of contacts with Turkish soldiers and imams during the Korean War. Its members number a few thousand, mostly converts in Seoul and Busan.

The federation follows mainstream Sunni teaching and seeks patronage from Saudi Arabia, Malaysia and other Muslim states to build a central mosque and send students abroad. It is loyal to the Seoul government and fiercely anti-communist, offering prayers for the reunification of Korea and hoping one day to bring Islam to the closed provinces of the North.

11.name: Halqat al-Khilafa
11.text:
The Caliphate Circle is a handful of Arab students in Pyongyang who pass around pamphlets of Hizb ut-Tahrir, smuggled in from Amman, Beirut and Damascus. Disillusioned by the defeat of 1967, they reject both Arab socialism and the Juche doctrine they are required to study.

They argue that only a restored caliphate can unite the Muslim world and free it from American and Soviet domination alike. Their numbers are negligible and their meetings clandestine, but the circle reflects the radicalization of Arab youth after the Six-Day War, and its members return home convinced that every secular revolution they have seen abroad is a betrayal of Islam.

12.name: Jama'at al-Talaba al-Muslimin
12.text:
The Muslim Students' Society gathers Egyptian, Syrian and Sudanese students and trainees in Pyongyang who share the ideas of the Muslim Brotherhood. Many come from families that suffered under Nasser's crackdowns, and they read the works of Hasan al-Banna and the recently executed Sayyid Qutb in secret.

They favour an Islamic order built through education, charity and gradual reform rather than revolution, and they reject the atheism of the host state. They maintain discreet contact with Brotherhood exiles in Europe and the Gulf, and their leverage lies in the professional networks they will carry home as engineers and doctors trained abroad.

13.name: Chosŏn Minjujuŭi Inmin Konghwaguk Naegak
13.text:
The Cabinet of the DPRK is the state's executive apparatus, headed by Premier Kim Il-sung, with First Vice Premier Kim Il directing the ministries and the State Planning Commission day to day. Its economists and engineers manage the extended Seven-Year Plan, whose targets slipped badly after military spending soared in the mid-1960s.

The ministries favour balanced growth, realistic targets, imports of Western and Japanese machinery and calm relations with both Moscow and Beijing. They have no independent political base, but control over plans, supplies and foreign trade gives the bureaucracy quiet influence whenever the leadership must choose between military priorities and the people's living standards.

14.name: Chosŏn Kidokkyodo Ryŏnmaeng
14.text:
The Korean Christian Federation was established in 1946 to bring the North's Protestants under state supervision and is led by Kang Ryang-uk, a Presbyterian minister related to Kim Il-sung's mother. Most churches have long been closed, and the faithful worship in small house gatherings watched by the authorities.

The federation professes loyalty to the Republic, anti-imperialism and support for peaceful reunification, while trying to preserve a remnant of the once-thriving Pyongyang Protestant community. It serves the regime abroad as proof of religious tolerance, yet it also shelters the families of believers who still remember the city as the Jerusalem of the East.

15.name: Chae Ilbon Chosŏnin Ch'ongryŏnhaphoe
15.english: General Association of Korean Residents in Japan
15.text:
The General Association of Korean Residents in Japan, founded in 1955 under Han Duk-su, organizes the pro-Pyongyang Koreans of Japan. Its members run pachinko halls, restaurants, trading firms and credit unions, and since 1959 the association has organized the repatriation of tens of thousands of Koreans to the North.

Chongryon channels hard currency, machinery and consumer goods to Pyongyang, finances Korean schools in Japan and lobbies Tokyo for trade. Its businessmen form the closest thing the DPRK has to a moneyed elite, and their remittances and gifts buy access to the leadership. They favour trade with Japan and the West, and stable conditions for business.

16.name: Nongmin Sijang
16.text:
The Farmers' Markets are the periodic peasant markets tolerated in towns and county seats, where cooperative farmers sell produce from their private kitchen gardens, along with eggs, livestock and handicrafts. Officials regard them as a remnant of the old society, yet they remain open because the state distribution system cannot supply everything households need.

The traders and farmers who depend on them favour larger private plots, freer prices and fewer restrictions on movement and trade. They have no voice in politics, but every shortage in the ration system pushes more people to the markets, and local cadres quietly profit from protecting a trade the official ideology condemns.

17.name: Kŭmsu Kangsan
17.text:
Embroidered Rivers and Mountains, named after the poetic image of the Korean land, is a loose circle of foresters, botanists of the Academy of Sciences and keepers of the scenic reserves at Mount Myohyang, Mount Kumgang and Mount Paektu. They have watched hillsides stripped for fuel and terraced for grain since the war.

They promote reforestation, protection of rivers from industrial waste and the preservation of sacred mountains as national treasures. Their influence is limited to technical advice and the mass tree-planting campaigns the party organizes each spring, yet their warnings about erosion and flooding carry weight in a country where farmland is scarce.

18.name: T'ongil Hyŏngmyŏngdang
18.text:
The Revolutionary Party for Reunification is the underground party founded in South Korea in 1964 with Pyongyang's support. Its network was broken by the Korean Central Intelligence Agency in 1968, and its leader Kim Jong-tae was executed in July 1969; surviving cells and a central committee are sustained from the North.

It calls for a national democratic revolution in the South: the overthrow of Park Chung-hee, withdrawal of American troops, land reform and the nationalization of the chaebol-linked economy, followed by reunification. Its strength lies among radical students, intellectuals and workers in the South, and in the North's readiness to fund and broadcast for it.

19.name: Choguk T'ongil Minjujuŭi Chŏnsŏn
19.english: Democratic Front for the Reunification of the Fatherland
19.text:
The Democratic Front for the Reunification of the Fatherland was created in June 1949 as the umbrella of the Workers' Party, the Korean Democratic Party, the Chondoist Chongu Party and the mass organizations. Directed by the party's united front officials, it is the North's main voice toward the South and toward Koreans abroad.

Its programme is reunification through a confederation of independent Korea, free of foreign troops and great-power tutelage. It cultivates sympathizers in the South, in Japan and in the non-aligned world, and presents Juche as an independent path neither Soviet nor Chinese. Its leverage lies in propaganda, front organizations and diplomatic overtures.
19.wiki: Democratic Front for the Reunification of Korea

20.name: Ch'ŏllima Undong
20.text:
The Chollima Movement, named after the mythical winged horse that covers a thousand li a day, was launched in 1956 to drive post-war reconstruction through mass labour campaigns. Its Chollima work teams and model workers, honoured in factories and cooperatives across the country, remain the heroes of official culture.

Its activists embody a populist nationalism of speed, sacrifice and pride: Korea must catch up through its own effort, without depending on foreign aid or experts. They distrust managers who hide behind calculation, demand ever higher norms and glorify the ordinary worker, and their enthusiasm gives the leadership a ready instrument against bureaucrats and doubters.

21.name: Rodong Chŏngnong Chŏgwidae
21.text:
The Worker-Peasant Red Guards were established in January 1959 as a mass militia under the Workers' Party, and since the line of arming the entire people was adopted in 1962 they have grown to more than a million members. Workers and farmers drill after their shifts and guard factories, coasts and villages.

The militia embodies the fortress-state ideal: every citizen a soldier, every village a stronghold, and endless readiness for war with the United States and the South. Its political commissars preach hatred of the enemy and absolute devotion to the Leader, and its sheer size makes it the backbone of total mobilization.

22.name: Chosŏn Inmin'gun
22.text:
The Korean People's Army, founded in 1948, is one of the largest armed forces in the world relative to population. In January 1969 Kim Il-sung dismissed Defence Minister Kim Chang-bong, Chief of Staff Choe Kwang and other generals after the failed commando raid on Seoul, and installed Choe Hyon as Minister of People's Armed Forces.

The army demands priority for defence spending, fortification of the whole country and readiness for war with the South and the American forces there. Party commissars have been strengthened in every unit to prevent another challenge, yet the officer corps' control over men, weapons and a quarter of the national budget keeps it the second pillar of power.

23.name: Chŏnju Yi-ssi Wangsil
23.text:
The House of Yi ruled Korea as the Joseon dynasty from 1392 until Japanese annexation in 1910. Its head, Crown Prince Yi Un, returned to Seoul in 1963 after decades in Japan and lies gravely ill at Nakseon Hall in Changdeok Palace, attended by his Japanese-born wife Yi Bangja; his son Yi Ku, an American-trained architect, has returned with them.

The royal family has no political role and no restoration movement of any size, but it remains a symbol of Korean statehood older than either republic. Clan associations of the Jeonju Yi and conservative scholars cherish it as the embodiment of a united Korea before division, war and foreign occupation.
